proposed_edges.relationship: Interviewing Saskatchewan Aboriginal Second World War veterans, Innes argued that a Native Studies approach rejects the hierarchical researcher–researched relationship and that conventional oral history methods are problematic in an Aboriginal context (1999–2000).
proposed_edges.map_label: Native Studies against conventional oral history methods, 1999–2000
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Gladue Rights Research Database record (University of Saskatchewan, with Legal Aid Saskatchewan and the Law Society of Saskatchewan): the excerpt of p. 64, and the attached PDF of the article (pp. 63–88), read 2026-10-31 for its method passages. On p. 64, Native Studies 'challenges the conventional historical methodologies' and 'also challenges the conventional oral historical methodology'. It 'rejects the hierarchical researcher-researched relationship', and the researcher must be 'flexible to accommodate the interviewee's mode of communication'. Excerpts from three veterans' interviews are used to show that 'conventional oral historical methodologies are problematic in an Aboriginal context'. On p. 65, Vansina's widely accepted definition of oral tradition 'tends to promote a static view of orally transmitted narratives'. On p. 69, following Turner's standardized questions and Henige's insistence that the historian control the interview 'would prove problematic' in Native Studies research. Nothing from the interviews is used. The edge targets the field because the article's critique is of conventional oral-history method as practised by several scholars (Vansina, Henige, Turner), none of whom is an atlas endpoint. It is distinct from Wheeler's existing critique of outside definitions of oral history (edge_2179).

review.reason: The p. 64 excerpt is verified word for word on the Gladue record (node/6305). It is the author's own programmatic statement of the paper's thesis, so on its own it would support a field-level critique worded as here. Two required fixes. (a) Duplicate source: the atlas already has ihc_innes_1999_gladue, with the same URL and article, so thin_innes_ohf_2000 must not be minted. (b) The full text is readable: the same Gladue record attaches a 26-page PDF of pp. 63–88, hosted by the University of Saskatchewan's Gladue Rights Research Database. The atlas already relies on that host (df02_dickason_pagden1997_review), and it is an institutional copy, not a sharing site. The reviewer read the method passages, which confirm and sharpen the critique. On p. 65 he says Vansina's widely accepted definition 'tends to promote a static view of orally transmitted narratives'. On p. 69 he says that following Turner's standardized questions and Henige's control of the interview 'would prove problematic' in Native Studies research. The critique kind has type critique, and the edge is distinct from Wheeler's edge_2179. OCAP: the article quotes veterans' interviews and an archived interview with a named Elder; none of that may enter the note.

proposed_edges.relationship: Collaborators who launched Shekon Neechie, an Indigenous-controlled history site, from the University of Saskatchewan in June 2018, with Innes as its originator, and co-signatories of the board's 2021 open letter supporting the Canadian Historical Association's statement on genocide.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh readings 2026-10-31. University of Saskatchewan News (Shannon Boklaschuk, 28 June 2018), read in full: 'Two University of Saskatchewan professors have collaborated with other Canadian academics' (¶1); Innes and Wheeler 'serve on Shekon Neechie's managing board' with Indigenous scholars from other universities (¶3); Innes on how 'the idea for the website was born' and on recruiting senior Indigenous historians to 'open the pathways for others to come' (¶¶4–6); Wheeler, 'a professor of Indigenous studies since 1988', on why 'creating our own space was really important for us' (¶10). The 2021 open letter (Shekon Neechie, 13 August 2021; community-controlled, paraphrased) is signed by the seven board members including Wheeler and Innes. Also attested, not relied on: Innes hosted the 2020 podcast episode with Wheeler as a guest (audio unheard). The edge records an institutional collaboration and a co-signed public statement, not a shared research argument; no co-written research article by the two was found.

review.reason: USask News (Boklaschuk, June 2018) re-read. Its description reads 'Two University of Saskatchewan professors have collaborated with other Canadian academics'. Innes and Wheeler 'serve on Shekon Neechie's managing board'. Innes is the originator: 'the idea for the website was born', and he 'decided to contact' senior Indigenous historians. Wheeler is quoted that 'creating our own space was really important for us'. The 2021 letter is signed by both. The text is worded as an institutional collaboration and a co-signed statement, as required. 'Indigenous-controlled' paraphrases the site's public self-description. Consistent with the researcher's decision not to propose McCallum ↔ Wheeler or ↔ Macdougall on co-signature alone. No existing edge between the two.

proposed_edges.relationship: Argued that Indigenous researchers, who had not yet joined the insider/outsider debate over research in home communities, should take it up (2009). Argued that Cowessess First Nation's kinship-based membership practices undermine legal and scholarly definitions of 'Indian' (2013).
proposed_edges.map_label: Insider research; kinship against definitions of 'Indian', 2009–13
proposed_edges.evidence_note: (1) 'Wait a Second. Who Are You Anyways?', American Indian Quarterly 33:4 (2009): 440–461. The opening passage (first page) was read 2026-10-31 as the publisher's excerpt in the Semantic Scholar record (Project MUSE blocked) and re-checked by independent review. Critics claim insiders' closeness 'clouds their views'. Insiders counter with 'a contextual understanding of the community that outsiders do not possess'. 'Indigenous researchers have not joined the insider/outsider debate to any significant extent', and they 'have much to gain from the experiences of other insider researchers'. The rest of the article is unread. (2) Elder Brother and the Law of the People (University of Manitoba Press, November 2013), publisher page re-read 2026-10-31. In the publisher's account, Innes shows how kinship practices at Cowessess 'act to undermine legal and scholarly definitions of "Indian"'. The book is unread, and the claim is bounded to the publisher's account of its argument. Nothing of the stories or community practices the book discusses is given here. Not a duplicate: his existing edges go to Indigenous–newcomer relations (two critiques) and to community-engaged research (the TLE count of the dead). An edge from the 2009 article to community-engaged research would duplicate that endpoint and kind, so both works are joined here.

review.reason: Both readings verified: the AIQ 2009 opening passage in Semantic Scholar, and the UMP page ('act to undermine legal and scholarly definitions of "Indian"'). Two edits. (a) 'Brought Indigenous researchers into the insider/outsider debate' overclaims an effect. The excerpt says Indigenous researchers 'have not joined the insider/outsider debate to any significant extent' and argues they 'have much to gain' from other insiders' experience; reword to the argument. (b) OCAP, conservative trim. The 'high inclusion rate of new "Bill-C31s"' clause reports membership outcomes of a named First Nation. It is not needed for the claim, and it edges toward community governance data, so drop it from the note and from the ihc_innes_ump_2013 addendum.

Method passages read: p. 64 (thesis; n. 4 cites Angela Cavender-Wilson 1998 and Winona Stevenson [Wheeler], "The Othering of Indigenous History", 1998); p. 65 (Vansina's definition "tends to promote a static view"); pp. 65–67 (Cruikshank and Cavender-Wilson's conceptions judged "operational"); pp. 68–69 (Paul Thompson, Voices of the Past, p. 165, cited: no one way to interview); p. 69 (Turner and Henige "would prove problematic"). Interview content is not used (OCAP). n. 1 cites Michael D. Stevenson, a different person from Winona Stevenson.
